content: The document outlines detailed recommendations and guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment, and management of laryngeal cancer, including specific surgical and non-surgical approaches, preoperative and postoperative care, and follow-up protocols. 1. Laryngoscopic Examination and Voice Analysis in Laryngeal Cancer Diagnosis: Laryngoscopic examination is essential for early diagnosis in patients presenting with hoarseness. Stroboscopic examination is useful for evaluating suspicious lesions on the vocal folds. Narrow band imaging (NBI) and indirect autofluorescence endoscopy may aid in the examination of laryngeal cancer. 2. Role of Imaging in Diagnosis: Preoperative cross-sectional imaging studies, such as contrast-enhanced CT and MRI, are recommended for staging and pretreatment assessment of laryngeal cancer. PET/CT is particularly recommended for advanced-stage cases due to its superior ability to detect regional/distant metastases and secondary primary cancers compared to conventional CT or MRI. Ultrasonography (US) can complement CT/MRI by localizing the primary tumor and assessing cervical nodal status. 3. Preoperative Evaluation of General Conditions: For patients undergoing laryngectomy, preoperative pulmonary function tests (PFT) and arterial blood gas (ABG) levels should be assessed, especially in those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), advanced age, or significant comorbidities. For partial laryngectomy candidates, pulmonary status and exercise tolerance should be carefully evaluated. Screening for synchronous or metachronous secondary malignancies is recommended using modalities such as chest radiography, CT, PET/CT, and panendoscopy. 4. Management of Premalignant Laryngeal Lesions: Biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosing premalignant lesions. Mild to moderate dysplasia may be managed with either intervention or follow-up protocols. All grades of dysplasia should be followed up with regular monitoring. 5. Surgical Management of Glottic Cancer: For T1/T2 glottic cancer, transoral laser microsurgery is recommended for achieving acceptable oncologic and functional outcomes. Open partial laryngectomy may be considered for cases with limited extension into adjacent subsites or the anterior commissure. Total laryngectomy is the primary surgical modality for T3/T4 glottic cancers, though open partial laryngectomy may be an option in selected cases to preserve laryngeal function. 6. Neck Lymph Node Management in Glottic Cancer: Therapeutic neck dissection for N+ glottic cancer should include ipsilateral neck levels II, III, and IV. Elective neck dissection is not routinely recommended for T1N0 and T2N0 cancers but should be considered for T3N0 and T4N0 cases. 7. Surgical Management of Supraglottic Cancer: Conservative laryngeal surgery (e.g., open partial laryngectomy or transoral laser/robotic surgery) is recommended for T1/T2 supraglottic cancers. Total laryngectomy is the primary treatment for T3/T4 supraglottic cancers, though partial laryngectomy may be an option in selected cases without extensive invasion. 8. Neck Lymph Node Management in Supraglottic Cancer: Therapeutic neck dissection is recommended for N+ supraglottic cancer, including levels II, III, and IV. Elective neck dissection should be considered for clinically N0 cases, particularly in T3/T4 tumors or those with midline crossing. 9. Postoperative Risk Stratification and Adjuvant Therapy: Postoperative adjuvant therapy is recommended for stage III/IV laryngeal cancer and for cases with risk factors such as vascular invasion, perineural invasion, or multiple nodal metastases. Adjuvant chemoradiotherapy is recommended for patients with positive surgical margins or extracapsular nodal extension. 10. Rehabilitation and Psychiatric Support: Swallowing rehabilitation is recommended for patients with aspiration tendencies after surgery. Voice rehabilitation options, including esophageal speech, electrolarynx, and tracheoesophageal speech with a voice prosthesis, should be offered to patients post-total laryngectomy. Early shoulder rehabilitation is recommended after neck dissection to address potential dysfunction. Smoking cessation counseling and psychiatric consultation should be considered for all patients. 11. Postoperative Follow-Up: Patients should be followed up regularly for more than five years, with frequent evaluations during the first two years due to the high risk of locoregional recurrence. Regular laryngoscopic examinations are essential for detecting local recurrence. Imaging studies, including CT, MRI, and PET/CT, are recommended for baseline and ongoing monitoring of recurrence or metastasis. Thyroid function should be evaluated periodically, especially in patients who have undergone radiation therapy or thyroid gland removal. 12. Salvage Surgery for Recurrent Laryngeal Cancer: Total laryngectomy is recommended for recurrent rT3/rT4 cancer. Transoral laser microsurgery may be used as a salvage option for rT1/rT2 cancer. Open partial laryngectomy, particularly supracricoid laryngectomy, may be considered for recurrent rT2 and selected rT3 cancers. These recommendations are based on a combination of expert opinions, case series, and systematic reviews, with varying levels of evidence quality.
